1. INTRODUCTION
The  rapid  growth  of  software  development  has  made  collaboration,  source-code 
organization and version control important parts of modern computing. Developers 
often work on the same application from different locations or contribute at different 
stages.  A  repository  provides  a  structured  place  to  store  project  files  and  track 
changes, while collaboration workflows help contributors review and integrate work.
However,  the  terminology  and  workflows associated with  version  control can be 
difficult  for  students  and  first-time  developers.  Concepts  such  as  repositories, 
commits,  branches,  merges  and  pull  requests  may  initially  appear  complicated. 
Beginners may understand the purpose of writing code but remain uncertain about 
how to organize versions of their work, preserve earlier changes or collaborate safely 
with other contributors.
TESTBOOK  is  a  beginner-friendly,  Git-inspired  repository  and  collaboration 
platform conceived to make these workflows easier to understand. It provides a web-
based environment in which users can organize project repositories and files and learn 
the basic ideas behind collaborative software development. Its distinguishing feature 
is Beginner Mode, which presents technical concepts in simple language and connects 
each concept with the activity being performed.
The application follows a full-stack architecture. The frontend is built using React.js 
and  TypeScript,  with  Tailwind  CSS  for  interface  styling  and  React  Router  for 
navigation. Axios is used for communication with backend REST endpoints. The 
backend  uses  Node.js,  Express.js  and  TypeScript.  PostgreSQL  is  selected  as  the 
relational  database,  with  Prisma  ORM  providing  the  application-side  data-access 
layer. Authentication is designed around JSON Web Tokens (JWT), with password 
hashing using bcrypt or Argon2.
The project has been developed as an academic software application with emphasis on 
a  clear  interface,  modular  organization  and  beginner-oriented  explanations.  The 
frontend, backend structure, database integration approach, authentication architecture 
and principal repository and collaboration workflows form the scope documented in 
this report. The final testing and validation phase remains pending. Accordingly, the 
report describes the implemented design and development work while keeping test 
execution results unclaimed.

1.1 Background and Motivation
Students commonly practise programming through individual assignments and small 
team projects. As the size of a project increases, keeping multiple copies of files or 
sharing code through informal channels can make it difficult to identify the latest 
version. A structured repository workflow helps contributors maintain a  common 
project history and coordinate changes.
TestBook is motivated by the need to introduce these practices through a learning-
friendly interface. Rather than treating version control only as a set of commands, the 
platform aims to explain the purpose of each action and make the workflow more 
approachable for beginners.
1.2 Problem Statement
Beginners may face difficulty understanding repository organization and collaborative 
development workflows. Informal file sharing can lead to duplicate copies, unclear 
ownership of changes and confusion about which version should be used. There is a 
need  for  a  simple  learning-oriented  platform  that  combines  repository-related 
activities with explanations of the underlying concepts.
1.3 Scope of the Project
 Provide a web-based interface for repository-oriented project organization.
 Support structured management of repository information and project files within 
the application scope.
 Introduce version-control concepts such as commits and branches in beginner-
friendly language.
 Represent collaboration workflows, including review and pull-request concepts.
 Use a relational database and a separate backend API layer.
 Provide an authentication architecture to support user-specific access.
The  exact  production  deployment  configuration,  external  integrations  and  final 
operational  limits  are  subject  to  verification  against  the  running  application  and 
source repository.

2. OBJECTIVES
The main objective of TestBook is to develop a beginner-friendly web application that 
introduces repository management and collaboration concepts through an accessible 
interface.
1. To design and develop a responsive web-based application for repository-oriented 
project organization.
2. To provide a structured frontend using React.js, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS and 
React Router.
3. To develop backend services using Node.js, Express.js, TypeScript and REST API 
principles.
4. To use PostgreSQL for relational data storage and Prisma ORM for database 
access.
5. To design an authentication flow using JWT-based sessions and secure password 
hashing.
6. To organize project repositories and associated files through application modules.
7. To represent version-control concepts such as commits and branches in a manner 
understandable to beginners.
8. To introduce collaboration workflows, including the concept of pull requests and 
review of proposed changes.
9. To develop Beginner Mode explanations that translate technical terminology into 
simple language.
10. To maintain modularity so that additional features can be introduced in future 
versions.
11. To  prepare  the  application  for  systematic  testing,  validation  and  future 
maintenance.
2.1 Expected Outcome
The expected outcome is a functional full-stack application that demonstrates the 
design and integration of a React-based user interface, a TypeScript backend, REST 
communication and a PostgreSQL database. The platform is also intended to serve as 
a learning aid for students who are new to repository and collaboration concepts. Final 
confirmation of behaviour will be completed during the pending testing and validation 
phase.

3. PRELIMINARY SYSTEM ANALYSIS
3.1 Preliminary Investigation
Preliminary  investigation  was  carried  out  to  understand  the  difficulties  faced  by 
beginners while organizing code and working collaboratively. The project scope was 
framed around common learning requirements: storing project-related information in 
a structured manner, understanding the history of changes, separating work through 
branches and reviewing contributions before integration.
The investigation for this academic project was based on problem analysis, study of 
common version-control terminology and planning of the application workflow. No 
formal survey sample, interview count or statistical result is claimed in this report. If 
formal questionnaires or interviews were conducted, their details may be added here 
with dates and supporting evidence.
3.2 Present System in Use
In  a  basic  student  workflow,  source  files  may  be  stored  locally  on  a  personal 
computer and shared through email, messaging applications, removable storage or 
shared  folders.  Some  developers  use  general-purpose  version-control  tools,  but 
beginners may need additional guidance to understand the meaning of each operation 
and the relationship between repositories, commits, branches and pull requests.
These  approaches  can  work  for  small  tasks,  but  they  may  not  provide  a  single 
learning-oriented  environment  that  combines  structured  project  organization  with 
plain-language explanations.
3.3 Flaws in the Present System
 Multiple copies of the same file may be created when work is shared informally.
 It can be difficult to identify which copy contains the latest changes.
 Beginners may not understand how to preserve a history of changes.
 Collaboration  can  become  confusing  when  contributors  edit  the  same  project 
independently.
 Technical terms and command-based workflows may create a learning barrier.
 Informal sharing does not necessarily provide a structured review process.
11:
3.4 Need for New System
A  dedicated  beginner-oriented  platform  can  provide  a  more  structured  way  to 
introduce  repository  and  collaboration  practices.  TestBook  aims  to  combine 
repository-oriented  organization  with  guided  explanations.  By  connecting  actions 
with simple descriptions, the platform seeks to reduce the initial learning barrier and 
encourage disciplined project workflows.

4.1 Architectural Overview
The  frontend  is  responsible  for  presenting  screens,  collecting  user  input  and 
communicating  with  backend  endpoints.  The  backend  receives  requests,  applies 
application rules and interacts with PostgreSQL through Prisma ORM. The database 
stores  persistent  application  information.  Authentication  mechanisms  are  used  to 
associate requests with an authenticated user and restrict protected operations.
The architecture separates presentation, application logic and data persistence. This 
separation improves maintainability and allows the frontend and backend to evolve 
independently, provided that their API contracts remain compatible.

9. SYSTEM SECURITY MEASURES
Security is an important consideration for any application that manages user accounts 
and  project  information.  TestBook's  documented  security  approach  uses 
authentication,  password  hashing,  protected  backend  operations  and  validation  of 
incoming requests. The final implementation must be reviewed and tested before 
security effectiveness can be confirmed.
9.1 Authentication
The  application  uses  a  JWT-oriented  authentication  design.  After  successful 
authentication, a token can be used to identify an authenticated request. Protected 
backend routes should verify the token before allowing access to restricted operations. 
Token expiry, storage and renewal policies should be configured carefully.
9.2 Password Protection
Passwords should never be stored in plain text. A password-hashing algorithm such as 
bcrypt  or  Argon2  should  be  used  to  generate  a  secure  hash.  During  login,  the 
submitted  password  should  be  verified  against  the  stored  hash  using  the 
corresponding password-hashing library.
9.3 Authorization and Access Control
 Backend routes should verify that a request is authenticated before processing 
protected actions.
 Repository ownership and membership rules should be checked before allowing 
changes.
 Users should not be able to access or modify another user's private resources 
without authorization.
 Frontend  route  protection  should  be  treated  as  a  usability  measure,  not  a 
replacement for backend authorization.
9.4 Input Validation and Error Handling
Incoming data should be validated on the server even when client-side validation is 
also provided. Database operations should use the ORM safely, and error responses 
should not disclose  passwords,  tokens,  database  credentials, stack traces or  other 
sensitive implementation details.
28:
9.5 Data Protection and Backup
Database  credentials  and  authentication  secrets  should  be  stored  in  environment 
configuration  and  excluded  from  public  source  control.  A  suitable  backup  and 
recovery  procedure  should  be  established  for  the  selected  PostgreSQL  hosting 
environment. Backup frequency, retention and restoration should be documented after 
the deployment configuration is finalized.
9.6 Security Verification Pending
The  following  checks  remain  part  of  final  validation:  token  expiry  behaviour, 
unauthorized API access, ownership enforcement, password-hash verification, input 
validation, secret management and database backup/restore procedures. No security 
audit or penetration-test result is claimed in this report.

10. IMPLEMENTATION, EVALUATION & MAINTENANCE
10.1 Implementation Overview
TestBook is structured as a full-stack web application with a React and TypeScript 
frontend and a Node.js, Express and TypeScript backend. The frontend communicates 
with  backend  REST  endpoints,  while  the  backend  accesses  PostgreSQL  through 
Prisma ORM.
10.2 Development Environment
The  project  uses  Visual  Studio  Code  as  the  development  editor  and  npm  for 
dependency management. Git and GitHub are used as source-control tools during 
development.  Postman  is  included  in  the  development  toolset  for  preparing  and 
checking API requests.
10.3 Application Layers
Layer Responsibility
Presentation Layer React components, pages, forms, navigation and user feedback.
Communication Layer Axios-based HTTP requests and REST API contracts.
Application Layer Express routes, middleware, request validation, authentication and business logic.
Data Access Layer Prisma ORM models and queries.
Database Layer PostgreSQL relational persistence.
10.4 Evaluation Approach
The  application  will  be  evaluated  against  its  stated  objectives.  Evaluation  will 
consider  functional  correctness,  ease  of  navigation,  clarity  of  Beginner  Mode 
explanations, consistency of repository workflows, data integrity and responsiveness. 
These criteria will be reviewed during the pending testing phase.
10.5 Deployment Considerations
The application can be prepared for deployment by configuring the frontend build, 
backend  runtime,  database  connection  and  required  environment  variables.  A 
production deployment should use HTTPS, secure secret storage, restricted database 
access and suitable logging. The final hosting provider, domain, deployment URL and 
production configuration have not been specified in the project information used to 
prepare this report and are therefore not invented here.

12. CONCLUSION
TESTBOOK – A Beginner-Friendly Repository and Collaboration Platform is an 
academic full-stack web application designed to make repository organization and 
collaborative development concepts easier for beginners to understand. The project 
addresses common difficulties associated with managing project files, understanding 
version history and learning collaboration workflows.
The application is based on a modern web technology stack consisting of React.js, 
TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, React Router and Axios on the frontend, together with 
Node.js,  Express.js  and  TypeScript  on  the  backend.  PostgreSQL  is  used  as  the 
relational database, with Prisma ORM providing the data-access layer. JWT-based 
authentication and secure password hashing form part of the documented security 
approach.
A key feature of the project is Beginner Mode, which aims to explain technical 
concepts  such  as  commits,  branches  and  pull  requests  in  simple  language.  The 
modular  architecture  provides  a  foundation  for  repository-oriented  features,  file 
organization and collaboration workflows.
The  project  is  presented  as  developed  for  its  documented  scope.  However,  final 
testing, validation, defect correction and verification are still pending. The planned 
test  cases  and  validation  activities  in  this  report  must  be  executed  before  the 
application can be declared fully verified. After screenshots, actual test results, faculty 
details and final page references are added, the report can be reviewed for academic 
submission.
Through  this  project,  the  students  have  applied  concepts  related  to  frontend 
development,  backend  API  design,  database  integration,  authentication,  software 
architecture and technical documentation. The work also provides a foundation for 
future improvements in beginner-focused software collaboration.
